arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Medical-Grade vs Convenience Features
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two versions of a home monitoring device concept. Participants view a device description emphasizing medical-grade accuracy (T1) or convenience features (T2). They then indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).
arguments.sample: 400 U.S. adults recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. Randomly assigned to see either the accuracy description or the convenience description.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when accuracy is highlighted.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay when convenience is highlighted.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay for the accuracy version exceeds the convenience version by at least €10, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition built on medical‑grade accuracy. If the difference is less than €10, maintain focus on professional healthcare.

arguments.method: Online survey with simulated product offers and willingness-to-pay questions.
arguments.sample: 500 homeowners (aged 25-55) recruited via panel, balanced for region and prior outdoor power tool ownership.
arguments.measure: 1) Purchase intent: binary (would buy) or willingness to pay a premium (eur). 2) Primary reason: open‑ended rating on safety vs sustainability.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Safety‑focused offer will achieve at least 10% higher purchase intent than sustainability‑focused offer.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Sustainability‑focused offer will achieve at least 10% higher purchase intent than safety‑focused offer.

arguments.decision_rule: If safety‑focused offer meets the 10‑percentage‑point threshold, recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing safety and convenience. arguments.name: Fashion vs Thermal Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios.
arguments.sample: 300 US adults recruited via an online panel, stratified by age and gender to reflect the target consumer base.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and maximum willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 40% of respondents will express purchase intent for a thermal-regulating PCM garment, and WTP will be at least €50.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 40% of respondents will express purchase intent for a PCM garment marketed as fashion/status, and WTP will be at least €50.

arguments.decision_rule: If the proportion of respondents who express purchase intent for the thermal scenario exceeds the proportion for the fashion scenario by at least 10 percentage points, adopt T1. If the difference is less than 10 points, adopt T2. If neither meets the threshold, no expansion is recommended.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs. Eco‑Green Messaging
arguments.method: Online choice experiment with between‑subjects design. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: (A) Premium‑performance messaging (high‑end NASA‑developed, superior thermal comfort) or (B) Eco‑green messaging (sustainable, reduces energy consumption). They view a product description of the same flexible aerogel blanket and are asked to indicate purchase intent (yes‑no) and maximum price they would pay.
arguments.sample: 400 U.S. homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced for income, education, and environmental concern. Randomly assigned 200 to Premium condition, 200 to Eco‑Green condition.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary: intent to buy) and maximum price willingness to pay (continuous).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium condition will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Eco‑Green condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Eco‑Green condition will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Premium condition.

arguments.decision_rule: If the difference in purchase intent between Premium and Eco‑Green conditions exceeds 5 percentage points and the difference in willingness to pay exceeds €50, we conclude that the premium‑performance message drives higher adoption. If the difference is ≤ 5 points and ≤ €50, we conclude the eco‑green message drives adoption. If neither difference meets the thresholds, we conclude neither message is effective.

arguments.measure: Percentage of respondents who express intent to purchase (yes/no) and average WTP in euros.

arguments.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase scenarios.
arguments.sample: 200 self-identified hobbyist woodworkers (US and UK) recruited via panel, balanced for age, gender, and prior purchase of Festool.
arguments.measure: 1) Willingness-to-pay (WTP) for Festool at three price points (current premium price, discounted hobbyist price, and big-box price). 2) Purchase intent (binary: would buy). 3) Primary purchase driver (brand prestige vs. price).

prediction_by_theory.T1: WTP at premium price will be at least 20% higher than at discounted hobbyist price, and purchase intent will be higher when prestige is emphasized.
prediction_by_theory.T2: WTP at big-box price will be at least 20% higher than at premium price, and purchase intent will be higher when price is emphasized.

arguments.decision_rule: If WTP at premium price exceeds WTP at big-box price by ≥20% and purchase intent at premium price exceeds purchase intent at big-box price by ≥20%, proceed with differentiated hobbyist proposition (T1). Else if WTP at big-box price exceeds premium price by ≥20% and purchase intent at big-box price exceeds purchase intent at premium price by ≥20%, adopt unified range (T2). If neither threshold is met, maintain single range.

arguments.name: Home Monitoring vs. Clinic Visit Preference Survey
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized assignment to either a home-monitoring scenario or a clinic-visit scenario. Participants are recruited via a panel to match demographic and sleep apnoea status (e.g., diagnosed with OSA). They are shown a description of a non-contact sleep sensor (S+ or SleepMinder) and asked to indicate whether they would purchase it and at what price they would consider acceptable. After viewing the description, they are asked about their current method of sleep monitoring (clinic visits vs. home monitoring).
arguments.sample: 400 adults aged 25-65, recruited via an online panel, stratified by sleep apnoea status (diagnosed vs. not diagnosed). Target: 200 per arm.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent: binary (would buy) and maximum price willing to pay. Also, self-reported importance of reducing clinic visits (1‑10 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: If the home-monitoring scenario is shown, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than the clinic-visit scenario, and willingness to pay will be lower by $20 compared to the clinic scenario.
prediction_by_theory.T2: If the clinic-visit scenario is shown, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than the home-monitoring scenario, and willingness to pay will be higher by $20 compared to the home scenario.

arguments.decision_rule: If the home-monitoring scenario yields purchase intent ≥ 15% higher than the clinic scenario AND willingness to pay ≤ €150, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition for home use. If the clinic scenario yields higher intent, the test is inconclusive and further evidence is needed.
